Hanged
hăngd
v. (past of hang; in the Law the public exposure of an executed body under the curse of God — the statute Paul applies to the cross)
Past of hang, Anglo-Saxon hangian. In the Old Testament the word almost never describes the method of execution but the display of a body already dead: the criminal was stoned or slain and then hung up, so that the sentence was seen.

Biblical Definition

The key text is a statute about a corpse: “His body shall not remain all night upon the tree, but thou shalt in any wise bury him that day; (for he that is hanged is accursed of God;) that thy land be not defiled” (Deu 21:23). Two things are legislated at once — the public display of the curse, and a strict limit on it, since even a cursed body may not be left overnight to defile the land. Joshua obeys the statute exactly with the king of Ai, taking the body down at sundown. The narrative books use the word for judicial and poetic reversals: “they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai” (Est 7:10), and Absalom is found “hanged in an oak” (2Sa 18:10), caught by the head that had been his glory. Then Paul takes up Deuteronomy's parenthesis and puts the whole gospel inside it: “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree” (Gal 3:13). Peter preaches the same fact to the council: “whom ye slew and hanged on a tree” (Act 5:30).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives hanged as the past of hang when used of the execution or suspension of a person, and notes the scriptural declaration that he that is hanged is accursed of God.

expand to see more

HANGED, pret. and pp. of hang. Note. Hanged is used of persons; hung, of things.

HANG, v.t. To suspend; to fasten to some fixed object above, in such a manner as to swing or move.

2. To put to death by suspending by the neck.

Note. He that is hanged is accursed of God. Deut. xxi.

Note. Among the Hebrews the criminal was commonly first put to death, and afterwards hanged upon a tree as a public spectacle.

Key Scripture

Deu 21:23 — "His body shall not remain all night upon the tree, but thou shalt in any wise bury him that day; (for he that is hanged is accursed of God;) that thy land be not defiled, which the LORD thy God giveth thee for an inheritance."

Gal 3:13 — "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:"

Act 5:30 — "The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree."

Est 7:10 — "So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king's wrath pacified."

Modern Corruption

Penal substitution is dismissed as “cosmic child abuse”, which requires ignoring that Christ bore the curse voluntarily, in union with the Father's purpose, under a statute God Himself had written.

expand to see more

The charge, popularised by Steve Chalke and repeated across progressive evangelicalism, is that a Father who punishes His Son for the sins of others is guilty of an injustice no human court would tolerate. It misdescribes every party. The Son is not a third party press-ganged into suffering but God incarnate laying down His own life, of which He says “no man taketh it from me” (Joh 10:18); the Father is not venting wrath but executing a purpose the Persons formed together before the foundation of the world; and the sinner is not an innocent bystander but the guilty one whose penalty is borne. Gal 3:13 puts the exchange in one sentence: He was made a curse for us.

Deu 21:23 is what makes the exchange legally intelligible, and it is the reason the crucifixion was such a scandal to Jewish hearers. A hanged man is under God's curse by statute. When Paul cites the verse he is not softening the offence; he is claiming it — the Messiah went deliberately under the sentence the Law pronounced, so that those under the Law's curse might go free. Everything the modern objection finds intolerable is precisely what the apostles preached as good news, and the alternative theories of atonement that avoid it — moral influence, mere example, Christus Victor detached from substitution — leave the curse of Deu 21:23 standing over the sinner with nobody to bear it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Anglo-Saxon hangian; rendering Hebrew talah (H8518), to hang up, and Greek kremannumi (G2910), to hang, and xulon (G3586), a tree or wooden stake.

expand to see more

Hebrew talah (H8518) — to hang up, suspend; used of displaying an executed body (Deu 21:22-23; Josh 8:29).

Hebrew qelalath elohim — “the curse of God” in Deu 21:23; the hanged man is under a divine, not merely a civil, sentence.

Greek kremannumi (G2910) — to hang; epikataratos pas ho kremamenos epi xulou, “cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree” (Gal 3:13).

Greek xulon (G3586) — wood, a tree or stake; the apostles' deliberate word for the cross (Act 5:30; 10:39; 1Pe 2:24), tying Calvary to Deu 21:23.

Greek katara (G2671) — a curse; Christ is not merely cursed but made a curse, the abstract for the concrete.

Usage

"“He that is hanged is accursed of God” — a statute, and the reason the cross was a scandal."

"“Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree” — Paul claims the offence rather than softening it."

"“Hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared” — the reversal that runs through Esther."
